explanation: A passenger reads a newspaper with before-and-after photos of Hitchcock in an advert for a made-up diet drug, Reduco. He had lost a lot of weight himself.

claims.text: Lifeboat (1944) takes place entirely in a lifeboat.
In Lifeboat, Hitchcock appears in before-and-after photos in a newspaper advertisement for a fictional weight-loss product.
Hitchcock does not appear in Lifeboat as a floating body, on a passing ship or as a voice on the radio.
The weight-loss product in the advertisement is called Reduco.
Hitchcock had lost a large amount of weight by dieting shortly before Lifeboat was made.

evidence.restatement: Hitchcock's cameo is in a newspaper a passenger reads: before-and-after photos of him in a slimming advertisement.
He appears only in that advertisement, not as a floating body, a figure on a ship or a voice on the radio.

claimResults.note: Hitchcock said he had considered playing a floating corpse, which makes that distractor tempting but still wrong.

evidence.restatement: The fictional slimming product in the advertisement is Reduco.
Hitchcock had recently lost a great deal of weight on a diet, and his own before-and-after photos were used.
Lifeboat (1944) is set on one lifeboat for essentially its whole length.

claimResults.note: The film opens on the sinking ship's funnel before settling into the boat, so 'entirely' is the usual shorthand, not a frame count.

evidence.restatement: Hitchcock's cameo is a before-and-after photo pair in a newspaper advert for a fictional reducing product.
He does not appear as a floating body, aboard a passing ship or as a radio voice.

claimResults.note: The Reduco advert is his only appearance.

evidence.restatement: The advertised product is called Reduco.

issues.note: 'Takes place entirely in a small boat' is the standard description, but the first shot is the sinking ship's funnel. 'Almost entirely' would be airtight; no change needed.
